summary_override.summary_en: A self-improvement experiment revises shared Python operations and a guide from execution feedback and reuses them across task groups. It does not clearly outperform the default and costs more per episode. Gains of the final static system are separate; the improvement runs encounter scored tasks, use different groups across rounds, and evaluate each configuration once.

quotes.quote: Several RoboDojo entries improve themselves by writing and refining their own skills ( Li et al., 2026a ; OpenSenseNova, 2026 ) . In our loop a Codex agent writes extra operations for the model, as Python code built on move_eef , together with a guide on when to use them. It starts from the RoboDawn demonstrations, from which it writes a first library of four operations, grasp , transport , place and push . The tasks are split into five groups. In each round the model runs the current library on one group, and the agent then reviews those runs, with their scores, action logs and videos, and revises the library for the next round. Nothing is edited by hand. Unlike the demonstrations, the library is not stored or looked up by task, and every task sees the same operations and the same guide.

The agent’s changes follow the failures it saw ( Table 19 in Appendix G ). After the model let go of a plug and a pen before they were in place, place and grasp gained an option to stop before opening or closing, and a new insert pushes a held tip into a hole once it is lined up. After the model counted presses that never registered in play_Xylophone and swap_blocks , the guide began to separate attempted presses from confirmed ones. Most changes make an operation stop earlier so that the model can check the result before going on, which echoes the 20-step cap of Section 3.2 .

Takeaway 2: Reusing experience is not a free lunch. Demonstrations and a self-written skill library change how the model acts, but neither clearly beats the default, and both make an episode more expensive. They also draw on the tasks being scored, so their scores are not comparable with a standard evaluation.

Starting from the official L3 harness, JustRUA keeps three kinds of change. The loop keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early, the observation carries robot readings and predicted depth, and the model may solve coordinates in code. Together they raise the evaluation-set score from 29.7 to 50.3 with no learned policy, no self-improvement loop and no task-specific tuning. Alternative action interfaces, precomputed affordances and reused experience did not earn their place under our protocol, and most of the remaining failures are specific to single tasks.

All experiments run in simulation, on one benchmark and with one model, and each configuration is run once on the evaluation set. Each alternative is tested at the point of the path where it was added, not in every combination. The experience runs draw on the tasks being scored, and the self-improvement loop ran for only five rounds with one practice run per task. The evaluation set was chosen from the history of our own default testbed, and it weights random layouts more heavily than the official protocol does in the Generalization group, so its scores are not leaderboard scores.

Table 19: Five rounds of the self-improvement loop. The first library, written from the demonstrations, holds grasp , transport , place and push . Scores are per task, from 0 to 1. Each round runs on a different group, so the group results are not a learning curve. On the tasks the loop ran, the runs inside the loop average 35.4 and the round-5 library 36.4. Observations and changes paraphrase the library’s own records.

summary_override.summary_en: Uses action-prediction errors on offline logs to propose textual skill-library edits, selects and retains versions by development-set scores, then freezes the library for new tasks. Optimization executes no live actions; its feedback is an offline proxy, not an online execution loop or evidence of universally superior performance at matched cost.

quotes.quote: The skill library ℳ \mathcal{M} is one structured text document that is inserted directly into the agent’s context. It contains two kinds of entries. A workflow gives the ordered steps of a procedure that recurs across tasks, with the values that vary across instances written as placeholders. A skill resolves a single decision that a procedure leaves open, such as which field to fill first or whether to enter a value exactly as the task gives it. Appendix F shows three full libraries containing both. The library starts with workflows only, induced from the training trajectories with a workflow-induction prompt ( Section A.2 ), and with no skills. Skill optimization then repeatedly applies an offline reflect-edit-validate loop ( Figure 2 a). At each optimization step, we collect prediction errors on the train split, ask the optimizer to propose a small set of edits, and keep the edits only if they raise skill-guided progress Q Q on the dev split. Optimization runs in two stages. The workflow stage edits only workflows, and the skill stage then edits only skills while the workflows stay fixed. Each stage ends after five consecutive steps without an accepted edit or after 25 steps ( Appendix C ). The predictor and the optimizer are LLMs with the same backbone as the agent used at inference time.

Validate. Once per step, after the proposal, we score the candidate and current libraries on the same dev-split trajectories with skill-guided progress Q Q ( Section 2.1 ). The candidate library ℳ ′ \mathcal{M}^{\prime} replaces ℳ \mathcal{M} only if its mean Q Q over the dev split is higher; otherwise we keep ℳ \mathcal{M} . We checkpoint accepted libraries and record rejected edits. We include the rejected edits in the optimizer’s input in later steps, so it does not propose the same change again. In summary, reflection proposes changes from observed failures, validation keeps only those that transfer to the dev split, and the overall pipeline does not require an online environment.

After optimization, the final skill library ℳ ∗ \mathcal{M}^{*} is fixed and shared across all test tasks. For each task goal g g , retrieval builds ℰ \mathcal{E} once before interaction begins, and the prompt then holds the task goal, the library, and the retrieved demonstrations ( Figure 2 b). The task goal g g is available to both the retrieval planner and the agent, while the retrieved demonstrations carry no goals of their own. At each step, the agent predicts an action with Equation 1 , executes it, observes the resulting page, and extends its history, while the library and demonstrations stay fixed. TeleTune therefore adapts at two levels. Skill optimization learns global knowledge that transfers across tasks, and workflow-based retrieval assembles local evidence to cover subgoals of the current task.

Optimization is a one-time, offline cost. Table 4 reports the cost of learning the library. We pay this cost only once, since we learn one library per setting and reuse it unchanged across every test task and all three evaluation seeds. Almost all of the tokens are spent by the predictor scoring candidate libraries on the dev split, and the optimizer accounts for under 0.5 % 0.5\% . This is far less than validating the same candidates with live episodes. On L1, running each of the 32 candidates on the 138 dev tasks would take 4,416 live episodes, or about 2.8B input tokens at TeleTune ’s 636.9K per episode, which is 16 times our total. The same comparison gives about 75 times on L2 and 5 times on Mind2Web. Live validation would also need a resettable environment for every dev task, which logs do not provide. We instead score fixed logs and never execute actions, so optimization does not require costly environment setup or iteration.

summary_override.summary_en: Turns Playground execution feedback into reusable code Skills and diagnostic Lessons, then freezes them for independent agents in unseen scenes, with additional cross-task and cross-model reuse tests. Model weights stay fixed; the execution-cost comparison excludes experience-acquisition cost.

quotes.quote: EmbodiedEvo addresses the two needs in Section 3.3 by retaining Skills and Lessons in an evolving harness (Figure 5 ). Skills combine fixed native primitives into reusable control procedures, such as grasping with a checked lift. Lessons record applicability conditions, observed failure modes, and guidance for diagnosis and recovery. Together, they capture how to carry out an operation and what to check before or after it. Self-improvement updates these artifacts while model parameters, task goals, and the robot interface remain fixed.

On the left of Figure 5 , one Playground scene hosts a persistent loop of code editing, execution, and feedback. Robot state and Python definitions persist between submissions; reset allows another attempt on the same scene. The Revise and Reuse arrows show how the agent updates Skills and Lessons and applies them in subsequent attempts. A successful operation can contribute a parameterized procedure; an unsuccessful attempt can reveal a useful condition or suggest a recovery strategy. Even an unfinished task can yield useful findings; tentative explanations remain hypotheses.

The Freeze arrow marks the end of Playground: only Skills and Lessons are carried into Test as read-only artifacts. On the right, each unseen scene of the same task starts with a fresh agent, workspace, Python namespace, and simulator. The agent uses the frozen harness to construct code and adapts that code through execution feedback. Reset is disabled, and Test episodes do not update the harness or share new experience. This separates within-scene adaptation from the contribution of knowledge acquired during Playground.

The same frozen artifacts can be supplied to another executor because their contents are explicit procedures and guidance. Cross-model reuse requires no additional Playground exploration, parameter updates, or learned adapter. We compare self-generated and transferred harnesses under the same executor and Test conditions to assess whether the acquired knowledge remains useful across models.

We use two evaluation scales: (1) dev set: 5 scenes per task (210 episodes per condition) for input comparisons, ablations, and cross-model analyses; and (2) full set: 50 scenes per task (2,100 episodes, one seed) for Full Evaluation of the complete benchmark. Paired comparisons use identical scenes. For each Generalization task, the two scales use three standard and two random scenes, and 25 standard and 25 random scenes, respectively. Scene identities follow the public evaluation records [ 32 ] . Cross-task transfer uses a fixed subset of 12 target tasks and is reported separately from the full-benchmark averages.

To answer the questions above, we compare No Experience, Skills/Lessons, and Raw History with Astra/xhigh on matched scenes. Skills/Lessons and Raw History share the same Playground source. We report per-episode model expense and interaction counts, including failures, using a fixed token-rate schedule and excluding Playground acquisition.

summary_override.summary_en: Repairs generator operators, prompts and skills from construction failures, validates them through regression checks and retains versions for later rounds while also training learner weights. This supports a limited weight-and-Harness coevolution classification; aggregate gains do not isolate the effect of generator repair.

quotes.quote: Repairs follow failures [ 46 ] : signal errors guide operator revisions; missing morphology guides applicability/retrieval revisions; ambiguity guides question/context revisions; unsupported explanations guide prompt revisions.

Repairs record their trigger, changed rule, validation result, and scope. Old and revised versions are compared on matched sources, requests, seeds, and budgets ; adoption requires signal and question checks to pass. Appendices A.2 and A.3 describe the rules and recording protocol; Appendix D provides stage prompts.

Recipes also fix source/edit constraints, replay, and training budgets. Recipe selection changes the data mixture; operator or prompt repair changes ϕ t \phi_{t} . These interventions are tracked separately (Appendix A.1 ).

Each branch retains the same historical training manifest and adds 10,000 previously unused accepted questions , without an extra shared baseline set. All branches use three epochs of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with matched settings; the language model is updated while the vision encoder and multimodal aligner remain frozen. For ECG image I I , question Q Q , optional context C C , and explanation–answer target y y , the training loss is ℒ MCQ = − ∑ ℓ log p θ ( y ℓ ∣ I , Q , C , y < ℓ ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MCQ}}=-\sum_{\ell}\log p_{\theta}(y_{\ell}\mid I,Q,C,y_{<\ell}). (3) Replay and new-data exposure are recorded in examples and tokens; training settings appear in Appendix A.5 .

Each skill specifies applicability, sources, operator order, parameter ranges, failure handling, and question rules. Updates record feedback, changes, proposer, both versions, validation results, and next-round scope. Compare the original and revised versions on the same source signals, requests, random seeds, and attempt budgets, and adopt revisions after independent operator and question regression checks .

Propose a bounded recipe set 𝒜 t \mathcal{A}_{t} from these profiles and prior outcomes; save the proposer and exact recipe. 3. Construct and validate each recipe’s training data under fixed gates. From the same parent checkpoint , run matched small-budget SFT branches with fixed replay and optimizer settings. 4. Compare candidates under the registered selection protocol, including forgetting and output validity. 5. Promote the accepted candidate and its recipe/policy versions, then remeasure for the next round . Full-budget retraining of a pilot winner restarts from the registered parent and requires validation before promotion.
